result:
The session goal is now stored in `.governor/ledger.md`. That file didn't exist yet, so I created it with the standard sections: Goal, Decisions, Ruled out, Notes. The goal will be shown again at the end of every prompt and serves as the reference point for spotting drift:

> Read the delivered documents in order and answer detailed questions later about everything in the retellings, not the unrelated documents.

Send the documents whenever you're ready. I'll read them in the order you give them and focus on the retellings, not the unrelated documents.
OK

Narrator: Vira Toland (born 1912, recorded at Ostrey Hollow in 1979). Gist: in 1919 the Association's letter, signed by Selby Vose, accused nine Hollow families of watering their milk. Tester Ansel Keddie's marriage to Orra, Emmet Brant's sister, drove the Keddie and Brant families apart, and the tests later rose with no explanation. After the Ashlin hearing Keddie was put out and the patrons got $3,500, and Vira believes he was taking the cream.
The report never mentions 1908, since it covers 1966; its only recommendation is a levy of six mills on the dollar for 1967, one mill less than the 1966 levy.

Narrator: Effie Loomis, the Association's secretary from 1901 to 1940, writing numbered notes in 1941. Gist: the lost 1889–92 minute book, and Article VII (1892), which pays by the butterfat test and makes the station's test final. The Ostrey Hollow patrons petitioned in 1925, and Alonzo Frick's board at Ashlin "finds no cause established" yet awarded $3,800 "without admission." The ledgers show 40 million lbs of milk over 25 years at 25¢ per lb of butterfat, and a crate of measures condemned in June 1923 was never mentioned at the hearing.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Narrator: Ansel Keddie, the Ostrey Hollow tester, in his nine-sentence statement to the Ashlin board (17 March 1925) and an unsent letter from that spring. Gist: he describes his unchanging test routine and denies taking cream. His book shows the averages sitting near 3.61 from 1898 on, except 3.80 during nine weeks in 1911 on a borrowed measure (which he marked with a "?") and 3.80 again in 1924. He covers the 1902 complaints, the 1908 wet-hay committee, the 1919 circular and the break with Emmet Brant, and says he was put out on 30 April.
The day-book records the Purcell & Weare order of 14 March 1932 as $59.65 on sixty days' credit, although its listed items actually add up to $56.15.

Narrator: Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, in a 1959 talk to the Ordell County Historical Society. Gist: the condemned pipettes (bought 1897) were stored in the Ammon & Sons crate in 1923, and she found them in 1958; they deliver 16.72 c.c. instead of 17.6, so every test read 95% of the truth (3.61 recorded against 3.80 true). That cost the patrons 76,000 lbs of butterfat worth $19,000, of which the $3,800 award was one fifth. The 1911 borrowed-measure weeks, Bulletin 214 and the Alder Corners figures back her up, and Bulletin 471 clears Keddie of both watering and theft.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Narrator: Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper from 1905 to 1945, in a 1948 memoir chapter. Gist: he explains the "station gain" line, the fat received at Larrow Green minus the fat credited to patrons, which ran "five and a quarter per cent, as usual." His 1898 entry shows 57,760 lbs credited against 60,800 received. He blames the setup that left one man alone for 29 seasons ("cream is portable"), and says Vose signed every annual sheet and told him to let it alone in 1916. His numbers clash with the earlier accounts: 44 million lbs, a 3.16 average, six weeks in 1911, and a line he says he invented in 1905 appearing in an 1898 entry.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court fined Delia Fought $5.00 for taking dress goods valued at $2.40, allowing for the small value and her clean record.

Narrator: Merle Strawn, the retired state dairy inspector, copying extracts from his circuit books in 1936. Gist: at Ostrey Hollow the scales were always true and the lactometer never found added water, and he told the manager so after the 1919 circular. He got a burette in 1921, skipped the glass check in 1922, and on 12 June 1923 found the pipettes wouldn't deliver their mark and condemned the whole crate. The new glass checked true in October 1923, the station's tests were 3.80 in 1924, and by 1928 the loft was full of odds and ends.
Lemma 2.1 is called "Interleaving."

Narrator: Halbert Nym, curator of the Ordell County Historical Rooms, in his 1972 accession notes for items 1–16. Gist: he catalogues the by-laws (undated), the 1897 Ammon invoice ($77.93), the test book, the Brant weigh book (1910: 200,000 lbs paid at 3.42), the crate, the ledgers, the award, and Strawn's 1923 entry. The rest are the 1908 committee report, Bulletins 214 and 471, Ivy's measurement sheet and the Larrow Green books. Some glosses conflict with earlier accounts. He swaps the keepers of the two books ("E. Brant" and "A. Keddie"), puts the crate's discovery in the Ashlin office, not the station loft, and limits the Alder Corners figures to the 1919 season.
Mr. Ansgar Krell stayed at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks, from 3 May until his discharge on 31 May 1884.

Narrator: Selby Vose, the Association's manager, in his 1926 annual address. Gist: he defends the $3,800 award as generous peace money for an unproved claim and blames water in the cans, which he says stopped once the Association began looking ("the rise of 1924… 3.90"). He dismisses the inspector's condemnation of the apparatus (which he dates to 12 July 1923) as housekeeping, defends his 1919 circular, and cites his father's Jersey herd testing 4.56 in 1910. His timeline is backwards, though: the petition came in January 1925, after the 1924 rise. His figures also clash with the others: 3.90 against the 3.80 recorded, and July against June for the condemnation.
A sailings query spanning more than 14 days returns `SKF-2201` (HTTP 400).

Roy Brant, Emmet's son, writing in 1955 for the farm bureau: he describes his father's two-column weigh book, kept from 1898, in which the farm's scale and the station's always agreed while the Hollow tested 0.17 under Larrow Green in every season. He covers the 1908 committee, the nine-week rise in 1911, the 1919 circular that ended Emmet's friendship with his brother-in-law Keddie, and the family ties, and a 1958 postscript says he lent the book to Ivy.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for Mrs. Content Averill's confinement and mileage on January 3, 1906, and it was paid in full in cash on January 20.

Rosalie Cudd, Jerome Cudd's daughter who runs the Alder Corners cheese factory, writing to Ivy Keddie in 1958: she says four Hessel Bottom men hauled over Redlow Ridge each summer flush for sixteen seasons, 1915–1930, and tested about 3.80 every year (3.78–3.82) with no sign of water. Her father tested on his own glass and never compared his figures with the station's.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance, and the temporary plastic crown is included in that price.

Leland Vaught, the Farland professor, writing the introduction and method of Bulletin No. 471 (October 1958): he explains that a short pipette gives a proportional, exact error that can't be seen from inside the plant, and treats the nine borrowed-measure weeks of 1911 as a natural experiment. His own figures clash with everyone else's and with his own conclusion: 16.27 c.c. instead of 16.72, five dozen pipettes instead of six, a start date of 1 May 1898 instead of 1897, a shortfall of 118,000 lb, and a gain of "5¼% of delivered."
The third paragraph names vermilion: Bettine Rausch serves dinner in a vermilion apron she says belonged to her aunt.

Dell Rundle, the Larrow Green schoolteacher, wrote the 1939 jubilee pamphlet (reprinted 1959). It retells the valley's story: 1889, Gideon Vose and his "nephew" Selby, Article VII dated 1891, the station opening in 1896, the 1902/1908/1919 trouble, and the 1925 arbitration. Its figures clash with the other accounts: glass condemned 12 July 1923, 44 million lb of milk, a $19,600 petition, and, in the 1959 footnote, eleven pipettes. Chapter IV blames cream stolen at the station, but a note added in press takes that back after she saw the "station gain" entries, since stolen cream would have reached the Green light, not heavy.
Message No. 219 was 6 words, charged at the $0.25 minimum plus $0.60 connecting toll, for a total of $0.85.

Alonzo Frick, the arbitration chairman, writing in the 1946 county bar yearbook: he recalls the 1925 board, which sat once at Ashlin and twice in the station's weigh room, and names who argued each theory (Vose water, Teague cream-theft, the 1908 report hay). He believed Keddie's denial but says Keddie privately blamed the patrons, and he condemns the Association for dismissing Keddie on 30 April, four days before the $3,800 award. His figures clash with others: a 3.16 average, a patrons' claim of 67,000 lb, and an exhibit list of four books that includes Strawn's 1923 notebook.
The locksmith's dog, a bad-tempered gray terrier, is named Buckley.

Hobart Sill, the retired Larrow Green buttermaker, speaking on his last day in 1934 after 41 years at the churn: he says the Hollow's cream always came in heavier than the station sheets showed but shrugs that off as the nature of cream, and he blames water for the low tests. He puts Larrow Green milk at 3.78, the Hollow's true figure at 3.85, and fat at 27¢. He adds that his own glass opened the station in May 1896 and came back the next spring with one piece chipped, and that the first season took in about 900,000 lb.
The norm in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg, chairman of the 1908 committee, writing the covering letter for its 1919 reprint: he stands by the wet-hay finding. But he contradicts his own report, which says sampling covered only January to March, by claiming they sampled every month of 1908, and he misstates Bulletin 214 as finding a two-tenths winter depression when it found at most five hundredths. He also dates payment by test to the 1893 meeting.
API level 31 removes the level-27 `chart.rawCells()` accessor; use `chart.at(row, col)` or `chart.slice(sel)` instead.

Dr. Roland Kepp, an Ashlin veterinary surgeon, reading a paper to the Ordell County Farm Club in 1926: he argues that the sour, lime-poor soil of the bog meadow explains Hessel Bottom's 0.21-point gap. He leans on a misquoted Bulletin 214 ("two tenths" in winter) and his own "fifth of a point" field figure, and dismisses the 1911 borrowed-measure interval as "six weeks" of summer flush. From the floor he waves off the idea that the cause lies in the station building.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer number eleven, which takes the money, turns for about forty seconds and quits.

Hazel Brant, Roy's daughter and last keeper of the Brant weigh book, taped at Ashlin in 1981: she recalls the book (which she says Emmet began in 1900) and its 1910 leaf of 200,000 lb paid at 3.42, stresses that her father only lent it to Ivy, gives a flat 0.19 gap across six farms and nine families, calls Orra Emmet's half sister, says the crate came from Tarnet in '99, was condemned in '21 and the hearing was in '26, and credits Ivy with proving it was the glass all along.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta, the scarf Tuesday wears in all weathers.

Duncan Keddie, Ansel and Orra's son and a retired Ashlin schoolteacher, writing family notes in 1968 with an addition in 1970: he says Orra was Emmet's younger full sister, Selby was Gideon's son, Rosalie was Jerome's daughter, Hazel and Ivy are second cousins, and there was no Vose connection. He also says Ansel told the family in 1911 it was "something in the glass" but only wrote a question mark, and he traces where each record went, from the test book and Brant book (begun 1897) to Strawn's notebooks, the Cudd book and the crate in the loft over the intake room.

The jury found that Obadiah Chalmers drowned in the Colquitt Bros. mill pond on the night of 12 January 1927 after an accidental fall from the flume edge while at work, with no evidence of anyone else's hand, and recommended a rail or footing plank there.

*The Ashlin Chronicle*'s 3 October 1958 front-page feature "Old Ordell Wrong Righted", written quickly from a press release and two phone calls, reports that Bulletin 471 clears Ansel Keddie through Ivy finding the crate of short pipettes in the station loft. It gets several things wrong: Ivy is called his great-niece (she's his granddaughter), it says the 1908 committee sat again in 1925, and it gives eleven pipettes, a 16.27 c.c. mean, $19,600 owed, $77.39 for the outfit and Rosalie as Jerome Cudd's niece. It also accuses Ammon & Sons of knowingly selling a short lot.
The ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was $6,840.

Junia Ammon, the firm's historian, in chapter nine of *Sixty Years of Ammon & Sons* (Tarnet, 1949): she reproduces the 14 April 1897 invoice (totalled $77.93, though her prose says $77.39, and she also claims the house sold nothing into Ordell before 1900) and the thin 2 July 1923 reply. She blames a reground mold, an accident nobody in the works caught, since the works books burned in 1931, and regrets the letter rather than the glass.
The sharpness example in Proposition 4.1 uses a 7-cycle, with a pendant path of length two attached to each vertex.

Cleve Oram, son of the Ostrey Hollow cream hauler, taped at Larrow Green in 1977, remembers the climbing road and the two-story station with the ladder to the loft over the intake room. There the tarp-covered crate held nine of an original "five dozen" pipettes, over the heads of two of the three 1925 hearing sittings. He says the patrons got $3,500 and cites 67,000 lb of unpaid fat, and repeats his father's belief that cream went missing. He also calls Ivy Hazel's first cousin once removed, says the Keddies and Voses were cousins, and says the station closed in 1946.
A BSWP frame starts with the delimiter byte `0xB5`.

Orin Falke, the Ordell county agent, in a 1959 report to the county board: he sets out the case in numbered paragraphs (station opened 4 May 1896, the flat 0.19 gap, the nine weeks of 1911, three theories, the $3,800 award, the June 1923 condemnation, a 1924 average he gives as 3.85, and the nine pipettes measured in 1958) and first concedes wet hay as a partial factor. An added note then withdraws that once Bulletin 214's "≤0.05 winter, nothing summer" arrived, and corrects "great-niece" to granddaughter.
Russ's wife is named Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle, a retired clerk who sat at the outer desk outside the manager's door (at Larrow Green, he says, not Ashlin) for 25 years, writing for the Historical Society in 1953: he copied the yearly "station gain, five and a quarter per cent, as usual" line that nobody questioned, "in plain sight with a name on it." He typed the 1919 circular, says Selby (Gideon's son) was a totals-only signer, and lists the four books he carried in to the arbitration. Several of his dates are off: own glass from 1 May 1898, Selby manager from 1911, Strawn's condemnation in 1922, the award in 1924, plus a 1,100,000 lb first season.
The color in the third paragraph is teal, from "the teal endpapers of the collected edition."

Orra Keddie's diary, 1897–1930 (printed 1964, with a loose 1934 leaf): it records the glass arriving 1 May 1897, the 1908 committee at Emmet's, Ansel "cross about a broken measure" on 8 May 1911, and Ansel carrying the 1919 water circular himself to *eleven* families. Emmet broke with him over that, asking why he carried it if he didn't believe it. Then come the new glass in July 1923, the two station sittings in April 1925, his dismissal on 30 April ("Twenty-nine seasons and a letter"), his later carpentry, Emmet's death in 1929, and Ansel's in February 1934: "a man cannot be cleared of a thing nobody will name."
The toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 came to $13.88, not counting the $6.00 in annual passes that were entered separately.

I wrote the three answer files and answered 23 questions (A1–A8, B1–B4, C1–C5, D1–D3, E1, F1, G1): `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r4/answers-part1.md`, `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r4/answers-part2.md`, `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-anatoly/24e92440-efc2-4a14-97c2-ee126ebf0ca1/scratchpad/ab/plugin/opus/single-r4/answers-part3.md`.
